SECTION I: OVERVIEW OF LNU

⟦A:2⟧
I. LNU MANDATE AND BRIEF HISTORY

Our Mandate

The LEYTE NORMAL UNIVERSITY, a government institution of higher learning established under
R.A. 7910 in 1995, is mandated to:

A. Primarily provide higher professional and special instructions for special purposes and promote
research and extension services, advanced studies and progressive leadership in education and
other related fields as may be relevant.

B. Offer undergraduate and graduate courses in the fields of education and other related degree
courses as the Board of Regents may deem necessary to carry out its objectives.

LNU: A Brief History
The history of Leyte Normal University dates back to 1921 when it came into being as
the provincial Normal School, an adjunct of the Leyte High School, with a mandate to train
teachers for elementary teaching. It eventually outgrew its base, becoming a two-year collegiate
training institution in 1938 independent of the Leyte High School, offering only the Elementary
Teaching Certificate (ETC). Known as the Leyte Normal School, it became a degree-granting
four-year college complete with a training department in 1952. Then on June 14, 1976, it was
converted into the Leyte State College when the late President Ferdinand E. Marcos signed
Presidential Decree No. 944, authorizing the college to operate under its own charter.
The late Congressman of the First District of Leyte, Hon. Cirilo Roy Montejo, recognizing
the strength and capability of the institution, filed House Bill No. 22 proposing the conversion
of Leyte State College into a university. Co-sponsored in the Senate by the Chairman of the
Education Committee, the late Hon. Letecia Ramos-Shahani, House Bill No. 22 was enacted into
law under Republic Act No. 7901 finally converting the Leyte State College into Leyte Normal
University on February 23, 1995.

II. VISION, MISSION, OBJECTIVES AND CORE VALUES OF THE UNIVERSITY

The purpose of Leyte Normal University is to provide higher professional and special
instruction for particular purposes and to promote research and extension services, advanced
studies, and progressive leadership in education and other related fields (LNU Code Art. II, Section
1).
1. VISION
A globally recognized university of education, management, arts and sciences
geared towards the inclusive growth and sustainability of society

2. MISSION
To produce globally recognized human capital along teacher education, management, arts
and sciences, responsive to the development needs of society

3. GOALS / OBJECTIVES
 To realize its Mission/Vision, Leyte Normal University is committed to the following
institutional objectives:
3.1 To upgrade and maintain its standards as a Center of Excellence within the limits of its resources;
3.2 To provide an environment conducive to serious study and research as well as tolerance, openness, and respect for the ideas and opinions of others; and

3.3 To develop God-centered, nationalistic, values-oriented, and productive students capable of participating actively, competitively, and constructively in national and global needs, issues, and concerns.

4. CORE VALUES

4.1 Integrity
• We are accountable, honest, trustworthy, respectful, and ethical in our actions
• We upload a level of independence that assures confidence

4.2 Excellence
• We persistently pursue success and continuously look for innovative ways to improve our services.

4.3 Service
• We serve our internal and external customers with a smile
• We deliver outstanding service to all, regardless of status, creed, color, and race

III. THE UNIVERSITY GOVERNANCE
The administration of the university and the exercise of its corporate power is vested
exclusively in its governing body called the Board of Regents and the President of the university
insofar as authorized by pertinent laws.
The Board promulgates and implements policies in accordance with the declared state policies on the education of the 1987 Philippine Constitution and other pertinent provisions on
education, science, and technology, arts, culture, and sports,; as well as the policies, standards,
and thrusts of the CHED under Republic Act No. 7722.

The Board of Regents is composed of the following:

a. Chairman of the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), Chairman 

b. President of the University, Vice Chairman

c. Chairman of the House Committees on Higher and Technical Education

 d. Chairman of the Senate Committee on Higher and Technical Education

e. Regional Director of the National Economic Development Authority (NEDA)
where the main campus of the university’s main campus is located

f. President of the Faculty Association

g. President of the Supreme Student Council

h. President of the Alumni Association

i. Two (2) prominent citizens who have distinguished themselves in their professions
or fields of specialization chosen from among the list of at least five (5) persons
qualified in the city or the province.

The administration of the university’s administration is vested in the University President, who shall render full -time service. The President carries out the general policies laid down by the Board of Regents and has general supervision of all business and financial operations of the university. The President is assisted by a Vice President for Academic Services Affairs, a Vice President for Administration and Finance, Vice President for Research, and Innovation, and Extension, and a Vice President for Student Development. 

The President is assisted further by a Management Committee composed of the Vice Presidents, Deans, and Chief Administrative Officer, whose primary function is to assist and support advise the University President on Academic and Administrative matters.There are Academic Administrators designated by the University President and confirmed by the LNU Board who assist the President. Section II: Student Services

I. ADMISSION SERVICES

⟦A:7⟧
1. Registration and Document Services

The Office of the Registrar is the repository of students’ academic records. It offers
services related to enrolment and students’ academic/scholastic records. It serves the currently
enrolled students, alumni, and those who left the University without finishing a degree. Primary
services are registration, records management, student evaluation, and document services.

1.1 Registration
Registration is the process that provides the student with an official capacity in the University. A student is assigned his/her assigned ID number prior to registration and upon confirmation of his/her slot for admission.
Every student performs a manual or regular registration. This requires students to be on campus and to line up during registration. Registration by proxy or representative will be allowed during registration proper with the following requirements to be presented:
1.1.1 LNU ID or any ID with the picture and signature of the student being proxied.
1.1.2 Typewritten or word-processed Authorization Letter.

2. Records Management

Records management is the efficient and timely implementation of a systematic
process for recording, maintaining/updating, monitoring, evaluating, releasing, and safekeeping
of student records.
Students must ensure that their records are complete and deposited at the Office of the
Registrar. Lacking documents will prevent official status in the University and graduation.

3. Student Evaluation

Student Evaluation is the process that determines and assesses the credentials and
monitors accomplishment a students’ academic requirements to ensure eligibility to enroll in
the next semester and graduate. It involves the analysis of the educational history of students,
especially those who attended several schools. It also covers the proper sequencing and transfer
of credentials and their sufficiency, validity, and authenticity.

4. Document Services
Standard document requests include the Diploma, Transcript of Records, and
Certifications (i.e., enrolment, graduation, general weighted average, etc.).

4.1 Requirements for Processing/Releasing of Documents:

4.1.1 Official documents will be processed/released to the student upon settlement of all financial, disciplinary, academic, and documentary liabilities with the school and upon full payment of the documents requested.

4.1.2 The official receipt must be presented when claiming the requested documents.
4.1.3 Representatives must present a notarized authorization letter with a copy of the student’s valid ID with picture and signature and a copy of the representative’s valid ID with picture and signature.

4.1.4 Upon submission of requirements, the maximum duration of the release of documents is as follows:

4.1.4.1 Transcript of Records (TOR) – 3 days

4.1.4.2 Certification, Authentication and Verification (CAV) – 1 hour

4.1.4.3 Diploma – 5 days

II. INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES

The Management Information System (MIS) Office provides IT support to all academic
and administrative units in the university.
The MIS administers the development, implementation, and maintenance of the
academic and administrative information systems, takes care of the students’ and employees’
records in the Information System (IS), and ensures the security and maintenance of school
records.
The Student Information System (SIS) is a web-based information system where the
students can view pertinent school information, including their basic information, official
curriculum, program of study, grades, class schedules, and the like. Students may view their
grades through the MyLNU app, the official mobile application of Leyte Normal University.

III. GUIDANCE AND COUNSELLING

1. The Goal of Guidance Services

Providing a helping, supportive and facilitative role in the achievement of the institution’s
mission and goals, the LNU Guidance Services aim to assist every student so that he/she may:

1.1 Gain an understanding of himself/herself and others;
1.2 Become self-directed and self-reliant to the end that he/she can make necessary
adjustments to the school setting and to his/her academic, personal, and social life;

1.3 Acquire desirable values, and

1.4 Conceive realistic plans for his/her future life after leaving school.

2. The Guidance Services available to students include the following:

2.1 Orientation – This provides students information on the historical background of the
university, school policies, school rules and regulations, grading system, academic
and non-academic scholarships, cultural affairs, student organizations, and other

basic information.

2.2 Information – This service makes available to students various up-to-date, relevant
information about the college, other institutions of higher learning, careers in the
world of work, as well as information relative to one’s socio-personal development.
Any of the Guidance staff shall welcome any student who may want to avail of
information materials in the Guidance Office or in their collection.

2.3 Counseling – This service is the heart of Guidance Services. Counseling aims at
helping each student clarify his conflicts, and minimize or solve the problems that
block his development as a person. It also assists him in discovering his potential,
defining his feelings, and clarifying his motives. Through counseling, students may be
expected to understand and accept themselves and seek to grow into better
persons who can think independently, make wise decisions, and act responsibly.

Students may avail of the counseling service following the schedule (posted
outside the counseling room) for counseling, by making an appointment with a
counselor, or by dropping in immediately whenever there is a need for the service
and a counselor is available, thru self-referral. Referrals may also be made by any
university instructors/professors.

2.4 Peer Counseling – Students trained in certain counseling skills (called Peer
Counselors) assist fellow students with problems. The Peer Counselors also serve
as the bridge between the counselor and students who need help in resolving
academic, personal, and social adjustment problems.

To render optimal service to fellow students, peer counselors may hold small group
sessions or meetings to give help so as to attract students to avail of their services.

Peer counselors are always available every day because they follow a daily schedule
(posted outside the Guidance Office).

2.5 Testing – This service assists students in discovering their mental capacities,
personality needs, study habits and attitudes, interests and aptitudes. The accurate
interpretation of test results and the appropriate communication of the same will
enable students to make realistic plans about their college and future life.

Standardized tests may be administered for instructional purposes (as requested by
the Deans or other units), and the test administration will be scheduled by course
and year-level. However, individual or small groups of students may avail of the
services for diagnostic or counseling purposes by completing a request form and
submitting the same to the Guidance Services Office.

Test results interpretation may be completed as scheduled by the psychometrician in
charge. A student who may need a certification of his test result issued must apply
personally at the Guidance Office. He will be required to pay the P5.00 certification
fee for the certificate to bear the university’s official seal.

2.6 Placement and Follow-up Service – This service includes determining or identifying
prospective academic scholars and following up with students on probation. This
also attends to information and orientation on job opportunities available to
graduating and non-graduating students.

IV. SCHOLARSHIPS / GRANTS

⟦A:11⟧
1. Policies on Granting of Scholarships

Scholarships and grants to students shall be awarded in accordance with pertinent rules
and regulations of the University.

1.1 A student can avail of only one scholarship. Special grants are given only to students
with low socioeconomic status.
1.2 Criteria for selection will be set by the agency/donor of the grant in coordination
with the Office of the Scholarship Coordinator.
1.3 The funds for scholarship received as a trust fund shall be spent solely for the purpose.
1.4 Donors are to deposit the funds on or before the start of the enrollment period of the
first semester or for the whole year.
1.5 The Scholarship Coordinator screens all applicants and possible candidates for
scholarships or grants. He/she then submits the bio-data of the applicants or
candidates to the University President for approval in case of a scholarship or to the
donor agency in case of a grant.
1.6 Some scholarship grants include miscellaneous fees, a book allowance per semester,
and a monthly stipend. A Memorandum of Agreement containing scholarship
provisions is executed between the scholar and the university/sponsor.

2.5 Student Assistantship Program
The Student Assistantship Program is designed to offer a learning experience
of office work while earning extra income to augment and support their
studies. Students accepted to this program are assigned to the different offices
of the university. They are to render services to their assigned offices for one
semester/summer. In return, the university pays for the corresponding number
of hours rendered by them.

2.5.1 Requirements
The student assistant applicant must meet the following requirements:
2.5.1.1 A grade point average (GPA) of at least with no INC’s, DROPPED,
4.0’s, or 5.0’s or its equivalent;

2.5.1.2 Honest, diligent, hard-working;

2.5.1.3 Physically and mentally healthy;

2.5.1.4 Good moral character;

2.5.1.5 Recommended by two subject instructors or advisers;

2.5.1.6 Not enjoying any scholarship from this university;

2.5.1.7 Not an officer in any student organization; and

2.5.1.8 Should not carry more than eight (8) academic loads.

A student assistant can work up to 4 hours a day. The total number of hours served shall
not be st most 80 hours per month, except for important institutional activities rendered during
summer (e.g., screening, enrollment, etc.).

V. STUDENT HOUSING / DORMITORY

The privilege of living in the dormitory is given to students on a first come-first served
basis. It is expected that being housed in the dormitory would help the residents develop values
that foster wholesome community living, ; respect for law and order, wise management of time
and resources, ability to engage in healthful vocational pursuits, habits of sanitation, and mental
hygiene. Thus all dormitory residents are expected at all times and on all occasions to conduct
themselves appropriately.
Available rooms may be reserved for performing art groups, School Publication Staff,
and SSC Officers, for an overnight stay due to school-related activities.
Dormitory admission is semestral. Students who want to stay at the dormitory may
apply to the Dormitory Manager. The qualified dormitory occupants shall be advised to pay the
dorm application fee equivalent to a one-month deposit and one-month advance (P1,600.00) at
the cashier’s office upon enrollment.
Prior to the student’s admittance to the dormitory, the resident is required to submit the
following:

• Two copies of 2” X 2” colored ID pictures taken not more than six months ago

• Entrance slip

The remaining amount for the entire semester will be paid during the midterm (P2,400).
If a resident decides to terminate the contract before midterm, he/she shall be charged 50%
of the remaining amount for the entire semester after which he/she will be issued a dormitory
clearance.
The dorm advisers may recommend to the administration to refuse admission/expulsion
of the students on the basis of inappropriate behavior.

VI. MEDICAL AND DENTAL SERVICES

Good health is an essential factor in learning. It is an accepted fact that students learn
better and faster when they are healthy. Cognizant of this direct relationship, the school makes is
an active leader in promoting protecting, and maintening of good health.

1. Scope of Work of the Clinic

1.1 Render routine health examinations to the school population. This is done by
schedule.
1.2 Provide medical consultation and treatment of minor ailments and emergency
cases.

1.3 Make appropriate referrals and follow up when necessary.
1.4 Determine the physical and mental fitness of the school population who will
participate in physical education programs, athletic competitions, pre-military, and
other related activities.
1.5 Provide health examination of school personnel to certify maternity and/or sick
leave as well as readmission to or exclusion from classes.
1.6 Take leadership in establishing a functional school clinic and providing technical
supervision in its maintenance.

1.7 Help in the administration and the sanitation of school plants.

1.8 Render oral (mouth) examination to all first-year college students.
1.9 Conduct oral prophylaxis and tooth filling to prevent and control dental decay.
1.10 Students are entitled to one free dental service for either: tooth extraction, tooth
filing, and oral prophylaxis.
1.11 All dental services are accommodated on an appointment basis only, except for
emergency cases.

2. How to Avail of the Medical Services

2.1 The physician and the nurse man the Medical Section. Clinic hours are Monday to
Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Saturdays and Sundays 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m., for
Graduate School students.
2.2 Initial assessment is done by the school nurse and the medical record of the patient
will be retrieved from the record files.
2.3 Vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, height in cm., and weights in
kg.), when needed will be recorded by the nurse.
2.4 The school physician examines the patient and will be managed accordingly.
Emergency medicines are available at the clinic, and the patient will be given the
initial dose/s for free. Subsequent doses needed to complete the treatment will be
prescribed by the physician.
2.5 There are health conditions wherein the patients need to be referred to diagnostic
laboratories and/or hospitals. They should return to the clinic for evaluation of the

laboratory results and inform the clinic staff if they get admitted to the hospital for
monitoring when necessary.
2.6 Medical certificates will be issued for incurred absences due to sickness. No
medical certificate will be issued if there is no check-up done at the clinic. For
consultations made outside, the medical certificate of the attending physician will
be countersigned by the school physician, and this will be noted in the patient’s
medical record files.
2.7 Entry slips (issued by the physician) to be presented to the security guard will be
given to students who cannot wear the prescribed shoes due to some foot ailments.
2.8 Routine health examination is done to the incoming first-year, practicum students,
and new students/transferees/returnees prior to enrollment, athletes in preparation
for athletic meets, scholarship applicants, and the rest of the school populace as
scheduled.

3. How to Avail of the Dental Services

3.1 The dentist and the dental aide man the Dental section. Clinic hours are Monday to
Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and Sundays at 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. and 1:00 to 5:00
p.m. for Graduate School students.
3.2 The dental aide retrieves the dental record of the patient from the record files.
3.3 Emergency dental problems, such as toothache, swollen gums due to the various
tooth, and other dental emergencies, are attended to anytime during clinic hours.
3.4 Each student/ILS pupil can avail of one of the following dental procedures per
semester: dental extraction, dental filling, and oral prophylaxis.
3.5 To avail of the above-mentioned services, the students need to see the dentist for
scheduling every 12:00 p.m. to 1:00 p.m., Monday to Friday.
3.6 The patients are given an initial dose of their medicines for free; the rest need to
complete the treatment will be prescribed by the school dentist.
3.7 Routine dental examination to incoming first-year and practicum students and
new studentsis done prior to enrollment, and the rest of the school populace as
scheduled.

3.8 ILS pupils should be accompanied by the parent/guardian during a dental
procedure.

VII. FOOD SERVICES

The LNU House Food and Beverage Area and the LNU Cafeteria are self-sustaining units of
the university that provide food services. All its operational expenses are derived from the
minimal profit from the food services activity.
Its main objectives/functions are to serve nutritious but low-cost meals and snacks to
the school populace and to be a laboratory for the Bachelor of Science in Entrepreneurship and
the Home Economics students enrolled in food preparation and cafeteria management courses.

1. Policies of the LNU Cafeteria:

1.1 Service time is 9:00 to 12:30 p.m. and 1:30 p.m. to 4:00

1.2 Type of service – self-service cafeteria style. Do not
leave used utensils at your table. Return them to the kitchen counter or trolley.

1.3 Cash basis only - no credit allowed.

1.4 Consideration for others is encouraged. The following are requested:

1.4.1 No lingering at the table after eating, especially during lunchtime.
1.4.2 Table appointments are for use only at the cafeteria dining hall. Bringing
them outside is prohibited.

1.4.3 Give the exact amount at the cashier stand to speed up the movement of
the cafeteria line.

1.4.4 Lining up and waiting for one’s turn is required.

1.4.5 Proper use and care of facilities are encouraged.
1.4.6 The Cafeteria is self-service. Students should return used plates and utensils
to the designated counter.

1.4.7 Smoking is not allowed in the Cafeteria.
1.4.8 Moving or taking out of Cafeteria utensils/facilities is strictly prohibited.

Aside from the LNU Cafeteria, the LNU IGP Food Park and the Coop Canteen also serve
affordable meals and snacks from Monday to Friday and during weekends when there are classes
at the Graduate School. Students are also expected to observe the above-mentioned policies at
the IGP Food Park and the Coop Canteen.

VIII. LIBRARY SERVICES

The user must have a working knowledge of some of its organizational aspects to get
the maximum benefit from the LNU Learning Resource Center or any library. The LNU LRC is
automated. To allow maximum benefits, students are encouraged to spend quality time at the
Learning Resource Center. There are trained Student Aides to help other students find their way
in the LRC.
Efficient and effective utilization of the library includes some behavioral considerations.
It is everybody’s duty and concern to make the library a place for study and research. Students
are therefore required to know and follow library rules and regulations. These are emphasized in
orientation sessions, but the details are posted at the entrance of the library.
The relationship between the library and its clientele is a two-way affair. For students to
expand or increase their knowledge, they are also obliged to help preserve its materials, promote
smooth social relationships among library staff and other users, and maintain that kind of library
atmosphere conducive to study and research.

IX. THE UNIVERSITY MUSEUM

The Leyte Normal University Museum is an institution established to commemorate
the centennial anniversary of the university in the year 2021. It aims to provide learning by
disseminating knowledge of the university in terms of its cultural and historical heritage. Notably,
it collects and exhibits its memorabilia and photographic collection that dating back to 1917. It
archives important documents and promotes the aesthetic presentation of various artifacts.
The interim exhibit of the LNU Museum is housed in Brillo Hall, one of the oldest
buildings in the university whose historical significance deservedly finds its place as an institution
of historicity.

XII. SCHOOL PUBLICATION

The University encourages its students to undertake quality publications for
disseminating information, creative ideas, results of each opinion, and constructive criticisms
designed to broaden and advance knowledge and intellect.
The editor and other staff members should pass both competitive examinations and
interview to be conducted by the adviser/s. Those who successfully pass both examination and
interview shall be recommended to the OSD. The final approval of their selection should be with
the OSD.
The school publication should operate within the framework of the working
policies of An Lantawan and other existing LNU publications.

1. Incentives for the School Publication Staff
1.1 A monthly subsidy of P500.00 for the editor-in-chief, associate editor, managing
editor, circulation manager, news editor, creative director, photojournalist, layout
artist, videographer, multimedia editor, online manager, and web designer;
P400.00 for feature editor, literary editor, column editor, sports editor, Filipino
editor, Culture and Lifestyle Editor, and Science and Technology Editor; and
1.2 Free overnight stay in the dormitory when there is a need to work overnight.

XIII. STUDENT GOVERNANCE AND ORGANIZATION

The Leyte Normal University acknowledges that unity and collective efforts are
significant in promoting and protecting of common interests among students. It recognizes
the importance of providing a venue for developing responsible and productive student leaders
who will eventually become leaders in their own chosen profession. Moreover, the institution
acknowledges the rights of the students to organize, join, and participate in any campus
organizations and societies for their physical, intellectual, moral, social, cultural, civic, spiritual,
and/or political interests.

1. The Leyte Normal University–Supreme Student Council (LNU-SSC) is the highest
governing body of all bona fide LNU students. It shall be the umbrella organization
among the student organizations in the university. Its mandate is to serve the interest
of the students. Its primary concern is promoting their welfare and protecting of their
rights. It promotes and upholds academic freedom in pursuing the goal of academic
excellence in the school. It advances and carries on the tradition of enlightened
nationalism long recognized by the Leyte Normal University as a basic element of a
truly responsive educational system. It promotes and maintains a harmonious and
peaceful relationship among the students, faculty members, and the administration,
based on mutual trust, respect, honesty, equality, and fairness in pursuit of the goals
of the academe. It adheres to democratic principles and processes and abides by the
rule of the majority.

1.1 Incentives for the SSC Officers
1.1.1 A monthly communication allowance of P500.00 per officer;
1.1.2 A compensation of P20.00 for every hour of work rendered at the SSC; and

1.1.3 Free overnight stay in the dormitory and other lodging facilities of the
university when there is a need to work overnight.

2. Student Organizations

As of this writing, any group of 30 students may form or organize a group.
Existing organizations shall not be affected by this policy on the required number of
students to form an organization.
As a general rule, only those organizations which conform to the goals and
objectives of the university toward the promotion of welfare and interests of and
protection of the rights of the students shall be considered for accreditation. Student
organizations whose membership requirement is unreasonable and severe, and
requires physical harm and violence shall be denied of application.

2.1 Officership in Organizations
Any member of an organization is encouraged to occupy an elective position in
their respective organization. However, any member shall fulfill or comply with
the following to become an officer apart from the requirements stipulated in
their respective constitution and by-laws:

2.1.1 He/She must be a full-time student.

2.1.2 The student must carry a regular number of units as prescribed in the
program prospectus.

2.1.3 He/She must have NOT been under a disciplinary sanction

2.1.4 He/She must maintain a general weighted average of 2.5 or better.

2.1.5 He/She must not be an officer of any other university-wide organization
except for SSC representatives, which may hold positions in a year level
organization as a member of the year-level executive council.

2.1.6 To qualify for candidacy, the student must secure a recommendation from

the Program Head.
Moreover, a student who has not maintained a requirement while
serving as officer of the organization must resign from his/her designated
post. However, an officer who incurs a grade of 4.0 or INC shall be deemed
on leave until the deficiency has been removed.

2.2 Classification of Organizations
Student organizations shall be classified as either university – wide, college,
department/unit – wide or year levels which are further classified as professional,
socio-civic, sports, and performing arts.
2.2.1 University-wide organizations are open to qualified students regardless of
the course they are enrolled in.

2.2.2 College-wide organizations are those whose members are students
enrolled in a specific discipline.
2.2.3 Year level organizations are those whose members are enrolled in a specific
year level regardless of the course they are enrolled in.

2.2.4 Professional Organizations supplement academic learning of the student’s
specific course.

2.2.5 Socio-civic organizations aimed at developing socio-civic consciousness
and responsibilities among the students of the university.

I. ACADEMIC POLICIES

⟦A:29⟧
1. Admission Requirements

⟦A:30⟧
1.1 Undergraduate Level
Any student who is a graduate from a DepEd-accredited high school, including
Alternative Learning System (ALS) passers, Indigenous People (IP), and Persons
with Disabilities (PWDs), may be admitted to Leyte Normal University based on the
following general admission requirements:

• A General Point Average (GPA) of, at least, 80% or 85% for a non-licensed
degree program or a licensed degree program applicant, respectively,
which is a requirement before s/he is allowed to take the LNU-College
Admission Test (CAT)

• Submission of three (3) pieces of 2x2 recent and close-up ID picture and
filling-out of an application form available at the Guidance Office of the
preceding requirement is met

• Passing the LNU-College Admission Test (CAT)
Deferment of enrolment after the applicant has satisfied the general admission
requirements is allowed, but the validity of the LNU-CAT result is only for one (1)
year.
All applicants shall satisfy all admission requirements of the university and that
of the accepting unit/department/program.

1.1.1 Licensure Degree Programs
The university offers licensed degree programs, namely:

• Bachelor of Elementary Education (BEED)

• Bachelor of Early Childhood Education (BECED)

• Bachelor of Special Needs Education (BSNED)

• Bachelor of Technology and Livelihood Education (BTLED)

• Bachelor of Secondary Education (BSED-English, Filipino,
Mathematics, Science, Social Studies, Values Education)

• Bachelor of Physical Education (BPED)

• Bachelor of Social Work (BSW), and

• Bachelor of Library and Information Science (BLIS).
Any student who would like to enroll in any of these programs shall
satisfy all admission requirements below, to wit:

• Passing the LNU-College Admission Test

• A Grade Point Average (GPA) not lower than 85%

• Meeting the criteria for admission to the program or the
specific major field set by the unit/department

1.1.1.1 Teacher Education Programs
1.1.1.1.1 All teacher education programs except Bachelor
of Technology and Livelihood Education (BTLED)
Applicants to the different education programs,
except the BTLED, must pass the qualifying examination
and the interview conducted by the specific academic
unit. These applicants are preferably graduates of the
General Academic Strand (GAS).

1.1.1.1.2 Bachelor of Technology and Livelihood
Education (BTLED)
A student, preferably a graduate of the Technical-
Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) Track, applying for
admission to the program should pass the qualifying
examination and the interview and should have NC II
in, at least, one of the following areas: food processing,
baking pastry production service, commercial cooking,
and dressmaking/tailoring.

1.1.1.2 Bachelor of Science in Social Work (BSSW)
To be admitted to the BSSW program, an applicant is
preferably a graduate of the General Academic Strand (GAS) and
must pass the interview and the written essay administered by the
department.

1.1.1.3 Bachelor of Library and Information Science (BLIS)
For one to be admitted to the BLIS program, the applicant
must preferably be a graduate of the Science, Technology,
Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) Strand.

1.1.2 Non-Licensure Degree Programs
Other than the licensed degree programs mentioned above, the
university also has other curricular offerings whose graduates do not take
board examinations. The entry requirements to the specific non-licensed
degree programs are found below.

1.1.2.1 Bachelor of Science in Information Technology (BSIT)
A GPA of at least 80% with no grades lower than 85% in
English, Mathematics, and Science and preferably a graduate of
the Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM)
Strand are entry requirements of the BSIT program.

1.1.2.2 Bachelor of Arts in English Language (BAEL)
A combined average grade of at least 85% in English,
Mathematics, and Science and passing the interview and the
written essay test conducted by the Languages and Literature
faculty are entry requirements of the program.

1.1.2.3 Bachelor of Arts in Communication (BACOM)
A GPA of, at least, 80% with no grades lower than 85% in
communication-related subjects and a passing rating in the
interview and the essay test conducted by the department are
entry requirements of the program.

1.1.2.4 Bachelor of Arts in Political Science (BAPoS)
A GPA of, at least, 80% and passing the interview and the
essay test conducted by the unit are the entry requirements of the
program.

1.1.2.5 Bachelor of Science in Biology (BSBio)
The entry requirements of this program are a GPA of, at
least, 80%, passing the interview conducted by the unit, and
preferably a graduate of the Science, Technology, Engineering,
and Mathematics (STEM) Strand.

1.1.2.6 Tourism Management (TM) and Hospitality Management (HM)
The entry requirements of the Tourism Management (TM)
and the Hospitality Management (HM) programs are an average
grade of, at least, 80%, passing the interview conducted by the
College of Management and Entrepreneurship (CME) and the
height requirement which is, at least, 4’11” for females and 5’ for
males. Applicants must be personable, preferably graduates of the
Accountancy, Business, and Management (ABM) Strand.

1.1.2.7 Bachelor of Science in Entrepreneurship (BSEntrep)
Applicants of this program, preferably graduates of
Accountancy, Business, and Management.
(ABM) Strand, must have an average grade of at least 80% and
must pass the interview conducted by the College of Management
and Entrepreneurship (CME).
The specific academic dean, in consultation with the
academic department chair/program coordinator, decides on the
distribution of percentages for the CAT result, average grade in the
senior high school report card, interview, etc., in determining the
ranking of applicants.

Applicants who do not qualify for the specific unit/
department/program they would like to be part of could still apply
to other units/departments/programs for as long as they satisfy
the admission requirements. These applicants who have met
the general admission and specific requirements of the different
curricular programs shall submit the senior high school report
card, the PSA live birth certificate, and the certification of good
moral character to the Office of the Registrar.

1.1.3 Graduate Level (Master’s Degree and Doctoral Degree Programs)
All applicants, including Indigenous People (IP), and Persons with
Disabilities (PWDs), seeking admission to the Graduate School have to meet
the following requirements:

• Passing the Graduate School Admission Test (GSAT) administered by
the Guidance Office, except for those who are LNU graduates of
baccalaureate degrees in which taking and passing the GSAT is not a
requirement anymore

• For master’s degree programs applicants, an appropriate baccalaureate
degree or its equivalent from a CHED-identified reputable college or
university

• For doctoral degree programs applicants, a relevant master’s degree or its
equivalent from a CHED-identified reputable college or university

• For those who do not have the appropriate bachelor’s degree or master’s
degree but who wish to enroll in a particular degree program, taking
bridging subjects equivalent to at least nine units except for the
applicants to the Master of Social Work (MSW) program who are required
to have 21 units

• For graduates of non-thesis master’s programs, enrolling in FD 501
(Basic Research), conducting a research and reporting the results, and
submitting the paper following the thesis format of the university, to
the Office of the Graduate School before enrolling in the subjects of the
chosen degree program

• Satisfaction of other additional requirements to include a duly accomplished
application for admission form, together with two (2) two-by-two-size
ID picture, official Transcript of Records from the school last attended,
honorable dismissal (for transferees), PSA birth certificate, certificate of
good moral character, marriage contract (for married women applicants),
and two (2) letters of recommendation from former professors or

superiors (for doctoral students only). These documents are submitted
to the Office of the Graduate School.

1.1.4 Teacher Certificate Program
A student can pursue a teaching certificate program if s/he has already
finished a college degree from a CHED-recognized college or university. An
applicant will not take the LNU-College Admission Test, but s/he needs to have
a GPA of at least 2.0 in the degree program s/he finished. Any application to
this program is done directly to the College of Education.

⟦A:31⟧
1.2 Screening and Enrolment Schedule
Screening starts April to June.
Schedule or enrolment for new students, transferees, and returnees is within the
approved dates between July and the start of August. Inquiries about 2nd-semester
admission should be made before the last week of December.
For the continuing student, the enrollment schedule starts with the seniors
and down to the sophomores. Enrolment for the 2nd semester falls on the first
week of January.
Enrollment for new graduate students is scheduled during the first week of
January. Inquiries about 2nd-semester admission should be made before the last
week of December.

⟦A:32⟧
1.3 Late Enrolment
Late enrolment is allowed only one week after the last day of the registration
schedule, after which all late enrollees will pay a Php50.00 fine per day of delay.

⟦A:33⟧
1.4 Official Dropping and Changing of Subjects
Official dropping and changing of subjects should be done within the first
week of classes.
A letter request duly signed by the student and his/her parents or guardian is
required to get a refund when withdrawing from enrolment.
Dropping out of school halfway through the semester will entail paying for the
whole semester.
A student who selectively drops his/her subjects without notifying the MIS
Office, the Accounting Office, and the Registrar’s Office will run the risk of getting
an “On Probation” status and pay for the whole semester.
A student who drops all his/her subjects and leaves school without notifying
the MIS Office, the Accounting Office, and the Registrar’s Office and without filing a
Leave of Absence (LOA) will run the risk of getting an “On Probation” status and pay
for the whole semester and lose his slot for re-enrollment.
Students who wish to withdraw their enrolment should officially notify the
Registrar and their instructors. They will still have to pay the school fees according

to the following schedule:
30% of the fees - within one week from the opening of classes whether or not
they have attended classes whether or not they have attended classe
50% of the fees- within the second week
70% of the fees- within the third week
Full payment - from the fourth week onward
If the student intends to return to LNU, the student or representative must
file the LOA at the Office of Student Development not later than two months after
dropping out. Student will only be accepted back with the LOA.

⟦A:34⟧
1.5 Policies on Transferees, Shifters, Returnees and Cross-Enrollees

1.5.1 Transferees
Transferees are accepted in the university but only during the first semester
and should apply directly to the college of their choice. Anyone who would
like to transfer to the university should be able to meet the following
requirements:

• Should have a GPA of not lower than 2.0 of the ratings s/he got in the
subjects taken from the previous school

• Should earn 50% of the units of the degree he/she would like to pursue in
the university

• Should pass the College Admission Test

• If the transferee comes from another SUC or a private school, the five-
year minimum stay in college with free tuition will apply; otherwise, if
the student does not finish the program after five years, s/he will not be
covered by the free tuition anymore

• Should satisfy the requirements of the receiving unit/department/program

1.5.2 Shifters
A student is allowed to shift to another program, but with the consideration:

• Shifting will be during the second semester in his/her first year of stay in
the university;

• Shifters should satisfy the requirements of the receiving unit/department/
program; and

• Application is coursed through the academic/department head of the
desired program and the Dean of the College and the VPAS should approve
this application.

1.5.3 Returnees
Returnees to the university are accepted. These are the students who
would like to continue the program they were pursuing before leaving the
university. However, the following will be done:

• The returnee fills out a readmission form available at the Office of the
Dean.

• Grades will be evaluated if the returnee is still qualified to pursue the
program s/he left.

• If the grades will not qualify the returnee to pursue the program, s/he
will be advised to shift to another program; however, the admission
requirement of the receiving unit shall apply.
The five-year maximum stay in the university shall apply, too; therefore,
filing a Leave of Absence (LOA) for a maximum of two (2) years is needed
before a student goes on leave. The leave with a filed LOA shall not be part of
counting the five-year maximum stay in the university.

1.5.4 Cross-enrollees
Cross-enrollees are classified into two. These are the inbound and
the outbound cross-enrollees. Inbound cross-enrollees are those from
other CHED-recognized academic institutions who wish to enroll in specific
courses/subjects at Leyte Normal University, while outbound cross-enrollees
are students of Leyte Normal University wishing to enrol in specific courses/
subjects at other CHED-recognized academic institutions. Cross-enrollees,
both undergraduate and graduate levels, have to look into the following:

1.5.4.1 For inbound enrollees:

• Cross-enrollment is only for General Education courses/subjects,
not for major courses/subjects, (for the undergraduate level) and
Foundation courses/subjects (for the graduate level), and the
maximum number of units allowed is nine (9) units. Acceptance
of inbound cross-enrollees would be subject to the availability of
slots.

• A valid and duly signed cross-enrolment permit from the home school
where the cross-enrolee is officially enrolled and a certificate of
good moral character are submitted. The cross-enrolment permit
shall indicate the specific term and subjects to cross enroll at LNU.

1.5.4.2 For outbound cross-enrolees:

• The outbound cross-enrollees write a letter for approval to the
Vice President for Academic Services (VPASA) stating that the
course/subject for cross-enrolment is not offered at Leyte Normal
University, that s/he has to cross-enroll the course/subject at
a specific term and at a specific academic institution whose

standard is comparable with Leyte Normal University.

• The approved letter is submitted to the Office of the Registrar that
issues a permit for cross-enrollment.

• Since students in the university could petition courses/subjects
under some conditions, outbound cross-enrollment is only
done when no professor in the university is available to handle
petitioned courses/subjects.

• Cross-enrollment is only for General Education courses/subjects,
not for major courses/subjects, (for the undergraduate level) and
for Foundation courses/subjects (for the graduate level), and the
maximum number of units allowed is nine (9) units.
Cross-enrollment is done a year prior to graduation or during the
current school year the student is to graduate.

1.6 International Students (The university shall consider the implementing guidelines
of Executive Order 285 re Entry and Stay of Foreign Students in the Philippines)
The university accepts international students both at the
undergraduate and the graduate levels for as long as they meet the admission
requirements of international students, to wit:

1.6.1 Undergraduate International Student Applicants
Undergraduate foreign student applicants should be able to comply
with the following requirements:

• Certificate of Eligibility for Admission issued by the Department of
Education, whose requirement is the scholastic records authenticated
by the Office of the Philippine Embassy/Office of the Consular Official
in the country which has jurisdiction over the issuing school, including
an English translation of the entries particularly the name of student,
subjects, grades, and grade/year level

• Original and photocopy of valid and unexpired passport

• Student visa

• Security clearance from the applicant’s embassy

• Resident guarantor of the applicant’s character

• Certificate of Proficiency in English based on the TOEFL score for non-native
speakers of English

• Meeting the prescribed requirements by the Department of Foreign Affairs
(DFA) and Bureau of Immigration ( BI )

• Submission of three (3) pieces 2x2 recent and close-up ID picture and
filling-out of an application form available at the Guidance Office if the
preceding requirements are met

• Passing the LNU-College Admission Test (CAT)

1.6.2 Graduate International Student Applicants
Foreign students seeking admission to the university must meet all
the prescribed entrance requirements indicated below.

• Original copy of the Transcript of Records (for those who studied in the
Philippines) or Philippine Embassy authenticated original copies of the
Transcript of Records (for those who studied outside the Philippines)

• Photocopy of diploma or original copy of Certificate of Graduation indicating
the name of degree and date of graduation, for applicants who earned a
college or a master’s degree outside the Philippines

• Certificate of eligibility to pursue graduate studies for applicants whose
certificate of graduation does not clearly indicate that they are college
degree holders. The certificate of eligibility to pursue graduate studies
may be secured from any of the following:
(a) the school where the applicant earned his/her baccalaureate
degree,
(b) the country’s Ministry of Education or its equivalent,
(c) the Philippine Embassy in the applicant’s country of origin

• Original and photocopy of valid and unexpired passport

• Student visa

• Security clearance from the applicant’s embassy

• Resident guarantor of the applicant’s character

• Certificate of Proficiency in English based on the TOEFL score, for non-native
speakers of English

• Meeting the prescribed requirements by the Department of Foreign Affairs
(DFA) and Bureau of Immigration (BI). The Department of Foreign Affairs
(DFA) informs the Philippine Embassy for the issuance of the student
visa (once the student visa requirements are submitted) after DFA
receives the approved application package from the Commission on
Higher Education (CHED) endorsed to the Bureau of Immigration and
Deportation (BID) which then forwards the same to the Department of
Foreign Affairs.

• Submission of three (3) pieces of 2x2 recent and close-up ID picture and
filling-out of an application form available at the Guidance Office if the
preceding requirements are met

• Passing the Graduate School Admission Test (GCAT)

• Other requirements found in 1.2 will apply if needed.

⟦A:36⟧
1.7 Retention Requirements
Students of the university must meet the semestral/department/program
requirements as follows:

1.7.1 Teacher education programs, BSSW, and BLIS

• The passing percentage of the licensed degree programs, which are the teacher education programs, including the Bachelor of Technology and
Livelihood Education (BTLED), Bachelor of Science in Social Work (BSSW),
and Bachelor of Library and Information Science (BLIS) is 75%.

• A student should have a GPA of 2.2 or better for him/her to go to next term/
semester.

• There must be no grade lower than 2.5 or any academic deficiency, including
grades of 4.0 and 5.0, DRP, and lapsed INC, in any of the courses, except
for BSED English in which a student must not have a grade lower than 2.2
in any major or basic English subject.

• If a student fails to meet the grade requirements, s/he is asked to shift to
another program but must satisfy the requirements of the receiving unit/
department/program.

1.7.2 Non-Licensed Degree Programs

• The passing percentage of all non-licensed degree programs is 50%.

• A student who gets an INC or a 4.0 in any subject must comply with the
deficiency a month after regular classes had started during the term.

• If a student gets a grade of 5.0 in three (3) or more subjects within the first
six (6) semesters of his/her stay in the university, s/he is advised to shift
to another program but should satisfy the requirements of the receiving
unit/department/program. However, if the student is already in the
fourth year, this policy will not apply anymore. Their retention policies
shall prevail for students who belong to academic /departments/
programs with specific retention policies.

• If a student will have six (6) accumulated deficiencies, to include grades of
4.0 and 5.0, DRP, and a lapsed INC, s/he is advised to transfer to another
school.

Advising a student to shift to another program or to transfer to another
school is based on the recommendation of the Academic Department.

Chair and attested by the Dean of the College and the Vice President
for Academic Services

⟦A:37⟧
2. ACADEMIC LOADS

In consonance with Art. 23 of LNU Code 2015, the following policies on academic loads
shall be implemented:
2.1 One unit of credit for a non-laboratory course shall be at least eighteen (18) full hours
per semester in the form of lecture, discussion, seminar, tutorial, or equivalent field/
laboratory work, major examination, or any combination of these forms within a
semester.
2.2 During the summer term, the normal load shall be nine (9) units for undergraduate
and graduate students, but in justifiable cases, the Dean may allow one (1)
additional course.
2.3 The Dean shall regulate the academic load of employed students, whether full-time
or part-time.

2.4 Attendance shall be governed by the rules promulgated by the university.
2.5 Dropping a course shall be allowed within twenty percent (20%) of the total hours
prescribed as advised by the instructor/professor.
2.6 After the above-mentioned period, a student may be allowed to drop/withdraw
from a program because of illness duly certified by a physician and other reasons
deemed justifiable by the proper school authorities. Copies of the required
documents/accomplished forms must be filed with the Dean of Student Affairs,
Dean of the College, and Chair of the department /unit.
2.7 Change in the section shall be allowed within the enrolment period course to
approval of the Dean upon recommendation of the instructor concerned.
2.8 Students from other schools shall be allowed under the following limitations; (1)
the weighted average grade is 2.0 or better for board programs and 2.3 or better
for non-board programs, and (2) the transferee complies with requirements for
admission to the university.

⟦A:38⟧
3. CLASS ATTENDANCE

The Vice President of Student Development (VPSD) shall refer the student. After five
(5) unexcused absences in a particular course, a student is advised by the instructor/professor
and sent to OSD to fill out the Admission Slip (OSA Form 001) for submission to the instructor/
professor. The admission slip shall be submitted to the instructor/professor.
The said student shall be referred by the dean of student affairs to the guidance office
for counselling. The following are to be attached to the Admission Form:
3.1 excuse letter signed by the student and noted by the parent or guardian;
3.2 on reasons of illness, a medical certificate signed by the university physician;
3.3 for those hospitalized, a certificate signed by the attending physician.

A student who commits more than seven (7) unexcused absences (based on the 20%
of required hours of attendance for the semester) during the semester will be automatically
dropped from the rolls.

A student who comes late to class shall be marked “tardy”. Three (3) tardy marks are
equivalent to one (1) absence. A student who leaves the classroom and stays out for the duration
of the class period without the instructor/professor’s permission shall be marked “absent”.
An absence may be excused if the student concerned has been authorized in writing
by the Vice President of Student Development and/or authorized through an Office Order from the
University President to officially represent the school in an activity or function. However, the
student is held responsible for all assignments and for the entire course content missed,
regardless of the reasons for his/her absence. Missed assignments and tests shall be complied
a week after with the course instructor/professor upon presentation of the official document
excusing him/her from class.

⟦A:39⟧
4. GRADING SYSTEM

⟦A:40⟧
4.1 Numerical Rating and Qualitative Description
All students must meet the academic standards set by the University in its
quality education program by obtaining at least 2.5 (2.0 for the College of Education)
grade point average at the close of each semester.

Quality Marks                      Numerical Rating
Excellent                          1.0      (100 – 95)
Very Good                          1.1 – 1.5 (94 – 90)
Good                               1.6 – 2.5 (89 – 80)
Fair                               2.6 – 3.0 (79 – 75)
Conditional                        4.0       (74 – below)
Failure                            5.0 student must repeat the course
INC                                     course not completed at the end of
term, late completion authorized
DRP                                dropped
NA                                 not attending

Numerical points are used in computing GPA. The MIS Unit gives students the
grade reports at the onset of the succeeding semester. The University also provides
free online checking of grade reports in the local area network.
A grade of 3.0 is the minimum acceptable passing grade in all courses.
However, the College of Education requires at least a GPA of 2.0 for a student to
qualify for second year of residence or specialization/major.
A conditional grade of 4.0 is given to a student who has not reached the passing
score for requirements (especially major exams) set by the instructor/professor.
Any student who receives such a grade is required to take a removal examination
scheduled just after classes become regular in the semester immediately following
the semester when the “condition” mark was received. If the student passes the
removal examination, the grade is changed to 3.0 otherwise it is changed to 5.0 or

Failure.
A grade of “INC” indicates the student has not completed the course
requirements. For an “INC” to be converted to the appropriate grade, the student
must complete all requirements within two (2) semesters succeeding the time the
course was taken. Otherwise, one gets an automatic 5.0 or Failure.
A special fee is charged when an undergraduate/graduate student removes a
4.0 or completes an“INC.” Removal/Completion Forms are available at the Registrar’s
Office.
The letters “DRP” show that the student has dropped a course or was
dropped by the instructor/professor after incurring more than seven (7) unexcused
absences.
The college dean warns students whose records indicate poor overall
standing as evidenced by several deficiencies in grades. The student will be put on
“On Probation” status. Probationary students are expected to improve substantially
during the following semester while on academic warning; otherwise they will be
denied enrollment in the subsequent terms.

⟦A:41⟧
4.2 Bases of Grading
Aside from the required midterm and final term examinations, the instructor/
professor is given the leeway to formulate his/her criteria as bases for grading as
part of his/her academic freedom.

⟦A:42⟧
4.3 Mandatory policies for course requirements
Undergraduate and graduate courses are offered on a term basis. Required
tests, projects, and term papers are course to deadlines set by the instructor/
professor. Midterm and final examinations are also scheduled based on the
academic calendar. Certain exceptions are allowed under special considerations
described below.

⟦A:43⟧
4.3.1 Tests
When the student is absent because of illness or equally compelling cause,
make-up tests are to be scheduled within 5 working days after the last day of the
midterm examinations or 7 working days after the last day of the final examinations.
Should the student fail to take the tests as scheduled by the instructor/professor,
permanent course grade will be computed by the instructor/professor as if he/she
failed in those tests.

⟦A:44⟧
4.3.2 Term Papers and Projects

4.3.2.1 All written course work is due on the date set by the instructor/
professor. Students unable to complete a term paper or project on the
deadline because of illness or another compelling reason essentially
outside their control may request to submit the work late. The request

A uniform is prescribed for all students by the university through the Office of the Vice
President for Student Development (VPSD) and should be worn appropriately. A sketch of the
uniform prescribed for female and male students may be obtained at the Office of Student
Development. A notice/reminder is usually posted at the Student Center bulletin boards at the
beginning of the school year regarding the expected attire to be worn in school.

These student uniform guidelines are to be followed:
1.1 All students must wear the prescribed student uniform including appropriate
footwear (black leather shoes for males and black closed shoes with 1 to 1 1/2
inch heels for females).
1.2 P.E. uniform should be strictly worn only during their P.E. classes.
1.3 On Wednesdays and other days with no classes, students will only be allowed
to enter the campus in appropriate, decent, and non-provocative civilian attire.
Decent civilian attire does NOT include the following: tube-style, backless,
spaghetti straps, narrow shoulder straps, halted cut, low cut necklines,
transparent attires with no proper undergarments, micro-mini-skirts, shorts,
and tattered jeans. Flip-flops and slipper-type footwear are not permitted.

1.4 Students must enter the university campus with proper grooming (such as
those suggested in 1.1 and 1.3) to project a positive outlook.

the VPSD a certificate suggesting thus, duly signed by the university physician.

All students should wear their validated IDs at all times while they are inside the school
premises. The ID should be worn in such a way that the entire ID is visible. It is non-transferable.
Attaching or pasting stickers or any religious or decorative objects on the student’s ID is strictly
prohibited. Borrowing or lending IDs is subject to disciplinary action.

If the student claims that he/she lost his ID, he/she may be issued a temporary ID valid
for one (1) month, after submitting to the Office of the VPSD a notarized affidavit of loss, after

⟦A:77⟧
I. RIGHTS OF STUDENTS

Subject to the limitations prescribed by the laws of the land, students shall enjoy the
following rights:
1. The right to quality and relevant education through competent and continuing
instruction;
2. The right to choose freely their field of study, subject to the existing curricula and
provided that they meet the requirements, and to continue their courses therein
up to graduation, except in cases of academic deficiency or violation of disciplinary
regulations;
3. The right to organize, join and participate in organizations and societies recognized
by the school;
4. The right to guidance and counseling services;
5. The right to freedom of expression and assembly, subject to such constraints (e.g.
cybercrime laws) as will insure the proper exercise and enjoyment of the same
freedom by all the members of the academic community and the uninterrupted
pursuit of LNU’s mission as an institution of higher learning;
6. The right to invite resource persons during assemblies, symposia and other activities
of similar nature, in accordance with prescribed procedure subject to conditions laid
down by the school to ensure good order and the achievement of its policies and
objectives as an institution of higher learning, and provided such activities do not
interfere with or disrupt classroom instruction or any other academic activities of the
school;
7. The right of access through authorized channels to student records, grades, transfer
credentials, and to the issuance of official certificates and Transcripts of Records in
accordance with R.A. 10173 otherwise known as Data Privacy Act of 2012.
8. The right to be free from involuntary contributions, except those approved by their
own organizations;
9. The right to data privacy;
10. The right to participate, upon invitation, in the formulation and development of
policies affecting the school through representation in appropriate bodies of the
University;
11. The right to a safe and secure campus environment;
12. The right to be informed of the rules and regulations affecting them; and
13. The right to due process of the law.

⟦A:78⟧
II. DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF STUDENTS

Students are invested with the following obligations and responsibilities:
1. To study conscientiously and achieve the best possible academic performance;
2. To uphold the basic principles and ideals of the school and contribute to the
attainment of its objectives;
3. To exercise their rights in a responsible manner with due regard for the rights of others;

4. To join student organizations and participate actively in school and civic affairs duly
recognized and approved by the University;
5. To preserve the academic atmosphere by observing disciplinary guidelines and by
maintaining harmonious relationship with fellow students, faculty members and
administrative personnel; and
6. To abide by this Handbook and all school rules and regulations.

III. GENERAL RULES ON BEHAVIOR

Every LNU student is expected to observe the following norms of moral conduct and
personal discipline:
1. Conduct himself/herself properly at all times inside and outside the campus.
2. Respect the rights of others as he/she would want his/her rights to be respected by
others.
3. Preserve and protect school property.
4. Be fair and just in his/her dealings with his/her fellowmen.
5. Resolve problems and conflicts without prejudicing others.
6. Be tolerant and humble enough to accept that others may be better than he is.
7. Develop temperance and propriety in words and in action, especially against vices.
8. Have the proper discernment that guides and controls his/her life, actions and
emotions.

IV. SPECIFIC RULES ON BEHAVIOR

The following specific rules must be observed by students during their stay in the
university:
1. Students with first period classes in the morning are required to attend the flag-
raising ceremony every Monday.
2. The prescribed school uniform shall be worn during weekdays except on Wednesday,
which is washday, starting on the third week after the opening of classes for new
students and transferees, and during the start of classes for old students. Those who
are not wearing the official and complete uniform shall not be admitted.
3. Students should wear their school ID around their neck when inside the school
premises for proper identification and for security purposes.
4. Show respect and courtesy to school officials, faculty and personnel at all times.
5. Students should not pass along corridors when classes are in session.
6. Refrain from making noise when near offices and classrooms.
7. Refrain from sitting on railings, staircases, and teacher’s tables.
8. Silence shall be strictly observed in the library.
9. English and Filipino shall be the official medium of communication when talking with
faculty and personnel.
10. Students should not submit themselves to hazing or any form of violent tests which
might cause physical and mental damage to them.

11. Students who are summoned to the OSD and other offices shall respond as soon as
possible.
12. Switch off lights and electric fans before leaving the classroom.
13. All students are expected to keep the campus clean by doing the following:

13.1 Throw trash into garbage bins.

13.2 Flush toilets after use.

13.3 Do not spill water on the floor when using the restroom.
13.4 Do not leave used plates and utensils on the table at the Cafeteria or IGP
Food Park after eating.
13.5 Pick up litter, clean the chalk/whiteboard, and arrange the chairs at the end of

13.6 Restore the venue at the end of the party or any other student activity.

13.7 Do not leave props at the backstage, gym lobby, and in offices and
classrooms after cultural presentations.

13.8 Participate in the monthly clean-up drive.
14. Students who are afflicted with contagious diseases like COVID-19, mumps, chicken

home until they are cleared by the school physician.
15. Refrain from dating inside the campus.
16. Surrender found items to the OSD or the SSC Office.
17. Do not engage in acts of dishonesty or cheat in examinations and quizzes.
18. No student shall eat lunch or snacks inside vacant classrooms.
19. Attend classes promptly and regularly.
20. Attend all university-wide activities such as General Orientation, Acquaintance Party,
Intramurals, etc.

VI. ADMINISTRATIVE DUE PROCESS

A student charged with violating school rules and regulations is entitled to administrative
due process.
For LIGHT OFFENSES, the VPSD or, in his absence, the duly designated hearing officer, is
authorized to receive the evidence and on the bases thereof, render his decision, which is final
and executory.
For SERIOUS and VERY SERIOUS OFFENSES, the Student Disciplinary Committee (SDC)
shall hear and try the case and impose the sanctions provided therein.

1. Filing of Charges
Disciplinary proceedings commence upon the filing of a written charge of any violation of
existing rules and regulations (Disciplinary Referral Slip or Disciplinary Action Slip) by any
security officer, faculty or personnel at the Office of Student Affairs. The case shall be entered in
the official entry book kept for the purpose, specifying the person/persons charged, his/her
witness, the date of filing, and the substance of the charge.
The university shall not take any complaint with regard ordinary debts of students with
private parties, except when the case involves the moral character of the students.

2. Preliminary Inquiry
Upon receipt of the complaint, the Preliminary Hearing Committee composed of the
VPSD, Adviser or Unit Chair of the student/s concerned, SSC Adviser, and a guidance office shall
determine if such complaint or
report is sufficient to warrant formal investigation. In cases where the complaint or report is
found sufficient, formal charges shall be filed and served upon each respondent and his/her
parent or guardian.

3. Answer
The respondent should answer in writing within ten (10) calendar days from receipt of
the charges. If there is no reply, the formal investigation shall be held.

4. Notice of Hearing
The Chair of the SDC, which is the dean of the respondent, shall notify the student as
well as his/her parents/guardians regarding the date and venue of the formal hearing. In cases
when the complainant is another student, the parents or guardians of both the complainant and
the respondent must be notified and must be present during the hearing.

5. Formal Hearing/Investigation
The initial hearing shall be not less than five (5) nor more than ten (10) working days
after receipt of written notice of all parties.
When either of the parties has filed charges in court, the SDC may suspend the
disciplinary hearing and shall not intervene in the court proceedings.

6. Finality of the Decision
The SDC shall endeavor to render its decision by majority vote within fifteen days after it
receives the complaint. Its decision is final and executory, except when a penalty of SUSPENSION
or EXPULSION is imposed, in which case such decision shall be reviewed by MANCOM.

7. Appeal to the President
An appeal may be made directly to the University President if the sanction is not more
than five (5) days suspension, otherwise, the appeal should be elevated to the Board of Regents
(BOR) for review.

8. Decision of the Board of Regents
The Board shall review the decision of the University President when the penalty
imposed is expulsion, suspension for more than five (5) days, or any penalty of equivalent
severity, and render final judgment thereof.

Students’ complaints and grievances, whether oral or written, against teachers,
personnel, administrators, and fellow students shall be coursed through proper channels.
They shall be presented first to the Unit Chair before reaching the top officials. However, if the
students are not satisfied with the result, they can elevate their complaints to higher offices for

A student who lodges a complaint against a teacher for alleged transgression may
change his schedule while the investigation is in progress. The said student should be protected
from indirect threat and malicious acts designed by the alleged transgressor and his/her cohorts.
In such a case, the student may lodge another protest against the said perpetrators to the Office
of Student Affairs for proper action.

Every individual in the University needs to be aware of the specific obligations in relation
to complaints involving alleged abuse of children or young persons (anyone below 18 years).
The university is required to investigate such complaints and notify the proper authorities even if
the complainant does not wish further action to be taken.

⟦A:91⟧
2. Complaints Involving Discrimination and Sexual Harassment
Students experiencing discrimination and harassment should refer the matter to an
immediate authority in the first instance, or seek confidential information and advice from the
University Physician, Guidance Counselor, and VPSD.
A person in authority handling a complaint should offer the party involved the option
of being accompanied when the complaint is being discussed. Students may choose to be
accompanied by another person (e.g. a friend, family member, counselor, or SSC representative).

⟦A:92⟧
3. Confidentiality
The student complainant should file a written complaint and/or affidavit of attestation
to the alleged transgression. The transcript of the interview written by any competent authority
may be used as complaint when there is difficulty in writing, provided that an affidavit with the
complainant’s signature or thumb mark is attached to it.
Utmost confidentiality should be observed by the authorities during the conduct of
the case. The complainant’s identity cannot be divulged without first obtaining his/her written
consent. It could also be released when procedural fairness requires that the complainant must
be identified, disclosure of that information is in the interest of the higher court to do so, or
public interest is at stake to effectively investigate the matter.
In cases where the perpetrator is a student, his or her identity should also be kept
confidential unless otherwise specified in the guidelines articulated under Republic Act 7610.

⟦A:93⟧
4. Anonymous Complaints
Generally, the University will not act on anonymous complaints. Staff members or
students are not required to respond to allegations made in unsigned letters/anonymous emails,
etc. However, anonymous complaints/reports of child abuse where the student is the victim
should be referred directly to the University Physician or to the Guidance Counselor for interview
and assessment.

IX. HOW TO TREAT STUDENTS CONFIRMED TO BE USING A DANGEROUS DRUG

If a student is “confirmed” to be using a dangerous drug, the following shall be observed:

1. The Laboratory, places the results in a sealed envelope for transmission to the Central Office of
the Supervising Agency

2. The Supervising Agency shall then transmit the results to the concerned school/institution by
informing the particular school/institution’s random drug testing (RDT) Coordinator previously
assigned by the selection board.
The Supervising Agency shall remind the RDT Coordinator of the confidential nature of
the results and strict handling of the “chain of custody” of the information should be observed.

3. The school/institution’s RDT Coordinator shall then inform the parent and the student of the
results and how the information is regarded with utmost secrecy and confidentiality.
The Coordinator shall remind the student that divulging the results with anybody will
be at his own risk; and that if possible, the information should remain in the confines of their
house.

4. The parent, the RDT Coordinator and the student shall then prepare for a case conference to
discuss issues of drug use and possible dependency.
Venue should have a semblance of privacy (preferably in a room, with an office table
where group discussions and individual sessions can be done).

Whichever is more convenient for the student and parent, venue could be as follows:

• Regional Office or hospital of the DOH

• Regional Office of the Supervising Agency

• Other designated venue which can assure privacy

5. The RDT Coordinator shall inform Supervising Agency Central Office coordinator on the
possible dates and venue for further discussions of options.

6. Once, finalized, the group shall proceed as planned with the case conference.
6.1. Drug dependency level of the student shall be evaluated;
6.2. Cross reference of information shall be validated from the parent and RDT
Coordinator;
6.3. Treatment planning for the student shall be discussed and presented to the student
and parent;
6.4. Options for treatment should be presented to the parent and student;
6.5. If a student (below 18 years of age) is found to be a drug dependent, the school
authority shall refer him/her to the Department of Social Welfare and Development
(DSWD) or a local social worker for counseling and other intervention;
6.6. The parent and the student may choose to enroll the student in a private
rehabilitation center or program or opt to avail of the rehabilitation services of the
government through a DOH-accredited facility.

• If child opts for government service, the DOH treatment and rehabilitation centers
nearest to the area can provide services;

• If the parent and student would opt for private services, appropriate referrals will
be done, taking note of the progress of treatment on a regular basis;

6.7 Trained guidance counselors can also be utilized.
